what_it_is: A flexible, practically inextensible cable (rope) of about 0.99 m, lying flat on the table (tracked points at z = 0.004 m, i.e. a cord of ~4 mm radius resting on the surface), with its first end fixed to the table at (0.05, 0) and its other end (point 20) held by the tool. The 20 tracked points are equally spaced markers along the cable (~0.052 m apart). The posts are fixed pegs the cable must be routed around (cable-routing / harness-routing task: wrap the cable on the prescribed side of each peg, then park the end at the target). The cable cannot pass through or over the pegs (on the table, pegs 0.08 m tall), so the side of each peg is fixed by the topology of the tool path. The 'load' is the pulling force (cable tension) felt at the tool: friction/drag of the cable sliding on the table, amplified when the cable is wrapped around and slides over pegs (capstan-like), plus a small residual at rest. 'Fights back when you hurry' = the drag is rate dependent: the faster the cable is dragged, the larger the tension, so the same path that is safe slowly overloads when done fast; also a tool that is blocked by a peg and then released rushes to catch up its servo reference and produces a huge spike.
evidence: layouts.npz: point 1 is at exactly (0.05, 0.00) in all 200 snapshots (std 0) -> fixed anchor; point 20 equals tool_pos to 1.4e-6 m.

layouts.npz: 3-D distance between consecutive points 0.0514-0.0526 m, total polyline length 0.9913-0.9954 m in all 200 snapshots, and the observation logs keep the length 0.992-0.996 m during motion -> inextensible cable of fixed length (~0.993 m).
layouts.npz: z of all points 0.0039-0.0040 m -> lying on the table, cord radius ~4 mm; z rises only to 0.0042 m in the violent spike of episode_906.
layouts.npz: rest load 0.23-0.85 N (mean 0.57) with no command -> small static reading.

episode_903 (success): load rises 3.9 -> 7.6 N while dragging at 0.117-0.120 m/s, falls to 2.1 N within 4 steps when the tool slows to 0.015 m/s (t=64), and to ~1.0 N when the tool moves back toward the anchor (cable slack) -> load is dominated by speed-dependent drag of the cable being pulled, not by position.

episodes 901, 902, 905, 907, 909 (overload ~10.0-10.5 N): the tool moves at a constant ~0.115-0.12 m/s; the overload occurs after the cable has been wrapped tightly around pegs (cable points at 0.025-0.033 m from a peg centre = touching it, peg radius 0.03 + cord 0.004) and is being dragged around them; load climbs 6 -> 9 -> 10 N along such a pull (e.g. 902 t=132..142: 3.8 -> 10.2 N; 905 t=104..116: 7.5 -> 9.8 N).

episodes 900, 906, 908 (spikes 10.8, 21.0, 11.2 N): the tool is blocked against a peg (tool centre 0.043-0.045 m from the peg = 0.03 + 0.015, in contact) while the command/reference runs ahead (lag grows 0.03 -> 0.17 m); when the tool slips past it rushes at 0.7-1.9 m/s and the load spikes -> peg collision + servo catch-up.
index.json: the two successes (903, 904) have max load 8.4 and 9.4 N, i.e. even the successes were within 15% of the limit at 0.12 m/s.

Geometry on the 200 snapshots (my planner, pure geometry): a tool path that passes each peg on the side opposite its required winding sign (pass on the right for +1) gives the required sides in 200/200 situations (min |W| 1.92 rad > pi/2) and the shortest cable configuration in that homotopy class is 0.70-0.85 m long, i.e. 0.14-0.29 m of slack against 0.993 m -> the final configuration is never taut; failures are dynamic (drag), not geometric. Posts are always ordered by x (0.38-0.72), targets x 0.61-0.90, start tool x 0.05-0.32.
why_the_existing_program_fails: It flies a fixed waypoint path at a fixed ~0.12 m/s with a fixed small clearance that loops tightly around pegs (overshoot and U-turn around a peg). Two failure signatures: (a) 5 of 8 (901, 902, 905, 907, 909): the cable gets wrapped around one or more pegs and is then dragged around them at full speed; drag tension grows with the length of moving cable and the wrap (capstan) and crosses 10 N - the speed never adapts to the load reading. (b) 3 of 8 (900, 906, 908): its path cuts through or grazes a peg, the tool jams against the peg while the commanded point keeps going, then the tool breaks free and races (0.7-1.9 m/s) to the reference, and the drag at that speed spikes the load (up to 21 N). The 2 successes (903, 904) are situations where the wrapping happened late / with little cable to drag, so the load peaked at 8.4-9.4 N, just below the limit.
unknowns: Speed was never varied in the observation material (always ~0.12 m/s commanded; only uncontrolled catch-up bursts). The load-vs-speed law (linear viscous? with a Coulomb part? an inertial part?) is therefore unknown; life 1 flies a load-feedback speed governor that sweeps speed and logs it so the gain load/speed can be measured in different wrap states.
Clearance around pegs was never varied (fixed in the existing program). How the load depends on wrap angle / clearance is unknown; I use a wider clearance and gentle curves, and will read the trace.

How fast the load reading responds after slowing/stopping (it decays within ~4 steps in 903) and whether stopping is always enough to relieve it, or whether backing off is needed; the governor includes a back-off branch that the trace will show.
Whether stick-slip of the cable over a peg can produce sudden spikes even at low speed.
Final settling: whether the cable's recoil disturbs the tool at the target (success needs |v| <= 0.02 m/s within 0.02 m).
